```plato
//==
// # Joints
//
// Impulse bodies for the constraint types in `joints.types.plato`. A joint is
// solved exactly like a contact — an effective mass along a direction, a target
// relative speed, an impulse that is the difference divided by the mass — and the
// two share the kernels in `rigid-dynamics.library.plato` (`DirectionalMass`,
// `SeparationSpeed`, `ApplyImpulse`) rather than restating them.
//
// Sections, in order:
//  - Anchors
//  - Distance and rope constraints
//  - Ball-and-socket constraints
//  - Springs
//  - Solving a set of joints
//
// WHAT IS HERE AND WHAT IS NOT. The two joints this file solves are the two whose
// constraint is purely POSITIONAL: a distance joint holds one scalar and a
// ball-and-socket holds three. The hinge, the slider, the fixed joint and the
// six-degree-of-freedom joint all additionally constrain ORIENTATION, which needs
// an angular error measured as a quaternion difference and an angular effective
// mass that is the inverse-inertia sum rather than a scalar. That is a coherent
// second piece of work and is deliberately not begun here; `RevoluteJoint2D`,
// `HingeJoint`, `SliderJoint`, `FixedJoint`, `GenericJoint`, `PulleyJoint`,
// `GearConstraint` and the whole limit-and-motor apparatus (`AngularLimit`,
// `LinearLimit`, `JointMotor`, `JointBreakThreshold`) are declared and unsolved.
//
// TWO CONVENTIONS GOVERN EVERY BODY HERE:
//
//   * AN ANCHOR IS IN ITS OWN BODY'S LOCAL FRAME, as `joints.types.plato` states,
//     and is taken relative to that body's CENTRE OF MASS. The two coincide for
//     every primitive `MassPropertiesOf` produces, which puts the centre of mass
//     at the local origin; a body whose centre of mass is offset from its origin
//     must have its anchors given in centre-of-mass coordinates.
//   * BODY INDICES MUST BE VALID AND DISTINCT. The static world is an ordinary
//     body with zero inverse mass, not the index -1 — the same rule the contact
//     solver follows, and for the same reason: it removes every case analysis
//     from the solve.
//
// Joints here are solved WITHOUT accumulation across iterations: each visit
// computes the impulse the current velocities call for and applies it. Contacts
// accumulate because their impulse is one-sided and must be clamped against a
// running total; an equality constraint has no clamp, so its increments simply
// sum and the accumulator would be bookkeeping with no consequence. The two
// one-sided cases below — a rope at its limit, a distance joint at its minimum —
// clamp their increment's SIGN, which is the correct one-sided treatment for a
// constraint that is either active or absent rather than saturating.

library Joints
{
    //==
    // # Anchors

    // The world position of an anchor given in a body's local frame, relative to
    // its centre of mass.
    WorldAnchor(body: SolverBody3D, local: Point3D): Point3D
        => body.Center + local.Offset.Transform(body.Orientation);
```
